lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: understand how varying carbon dioxide concentration, light intensity and temperature affect the rate of photosynthesis

primer.text: You know photosynthesis needs light, carbon dioxide and a workable temperature. This lesson explains why the rate still stalls: whatever resource is in shortest supply becomes the limiting factor, and each factor — temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide level, even chlorophyll amount — writes its own signature on the rate graph.

modules.title: Limiting Factors and Temperature
modules.opening: A plant can only photosynthesise as fast as its scarcest resource allows — that resource is the limiting factor. Temperature works differently from the others: warmth speeds collisions up to a peak, but beyond it the enzymes running photosynthesis denature, their active sites lose shape, and the rate collapses instead of climbing.
keyPoints: A limiting factor is something in short supply that restricts a life process.
The three main limiting factors are temperature, light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration.
Water is not treated as limiting because plants rarely run short for photosynthesis.
Warming raises kinetic energy, so reactants and enzymes collide more successfully.
Past the peak, heat denatures the enzymes and the rate falls away.
Chloroplast count can also cap the rate.

low.restatement: The scarcest supply sets the speed; too much heat wrecks the enzymes.
low.analogy: A bucket filled by its narrowest inlet pipe.
low.examPointer: Name the three main limiting factors, and add chloroplasts as the fourth influence.

medium.restatement: Temperature shows a rise-then-fall curve, unlike the plateau curves of light and carbon dioxide.
medium.analogy: Porridge: warm it and it cooks; overheat it and it burns.
medium.examPointer: Sketch the temperature curve with its optimum and describe denaturation at the fall.

modules.title: Light and Carbon Dioxide Curves
modules.opening: Light and carbon dioxide obey the same plateau pattern: raise the supply and the rate climbs, until some other resource runs short and flattens the curve. On the light graph the plateau arrives when carbon dioxide or temperature takes over; on the carbon dioxide graph, light or temperature does the capping.
keyPoints: More light gives the plant more energy for photosynthesis, so the rate rises.
The light curve flattens when another factor becomes limiting.
Carbon dioxide is a raw material, so more of it speeds the reaction.
The carbon dioxide curve also plateaus at the next limiting factor.
Both graphs are read the same way: rising limb, then plateau.

low.restatement: More light or more carbon dioxide means a faster rate — until something else runs out.
low.analogy: A tap feeding a tank: flow rises until the pipe's width takes over.
low.examPointer: Say which factor takes over as limiting on each plateau.

medium.restatement: The plateau's identity can be read by holding the other variables and asking which one is scarcest.
medium.analogy: A relay race slowing at its weakest leg.
medium.examPointer: Practise explaining plateau cause, not just sketching it.

modules.title: Chlorophyll as a Rate Influence
modules.opening: Chlorophyll is the pigment that absorbs the light energy photosynthesis runs on, and it lives inside chloroplasts. The more chloroplasts a leaf's cells pack, and the more chlorophyll within them, the more energy the leaf can capture per second — so pigment amount joins temperature, light and carbon dioxide on the rate's control panel.
keyPoints: Chlorophyll inside chloroplasts absorbs the light energy used in photosynthesis.
More chloroplasts mean faster photosynthesis in that tissue.
Pigment amount works alongside the three environmental limiting factors.
The palisade layer's packing of chloroplasts exploits this effect.

low.restatement: More green pigment, more captured light, faster rate.
low.analogy: More solar panels on a roof, more electricity captured.
low.examPointer: Tie chlorophyll to light absorption in every answer about it.

medium.restatement: Pigment sets the plant's light-capture ceiling; the environment sets where under that ceiling the rate sits.
medium.analogy: An aerial's size versus the broadcast strength.
medium.examPointer: Mention chloroplast number when asked for a fourth factor beyond the main three.

glossary.definition: A resource in short supply that restricts a life process.
The permanent shape change of an enzyme's active site at high temperature.
The green pigment inside chloroplasts that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
